blocks.text: — — — — now take up again your accustomed laments, and outdo the halcyons of the sea, outdo too the Pandionian birds. For your fortune is heavier than theirs. — — —

Thus, when the Pandionian birds return to their faithful lodgings and the home they left when winter drove them out, [II, 609] they stand upon their nests and recount to the roofs the beginnings of their old fate; and that broken and tearful murmur men take for words, and yet that voice is not unlike words.
— — — the Getic birds do not complain more to the hospitable roofs in broken speech.

Against these, however, it is objected that Plato, refuting those who say that swans θρηνοῦντας τὸν θάνατον ὑπὸ λύπης ἐξάδειν [thrēnountas ton thanaton hypo lypēs exadein], sing for grief as they bewail their death, says: Οὐδὲν ὄρνεον ᾄδει ὅταν πεινῇ, ἢ ῥιγοῖ, ἤ τινα ἄλλην λύπην λυπεῖται· οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἥ τε ἀηδὼν, καὶ χελιδὼν, καὶ ὁ ἔποψ, ὃν δή φασι διὰ λύπην θρηνοῦντα ᾄδειν [Ouden orneon adei hotan peinē, ē rhigoi, ē tina allēn lypēn lypeitai; oude autē hē te aēdōn, kai chelidōn, kai ho epops, hon dē phasi dia lypēn thrēnounta adein] (read οὓς δὴ φ. δ. λ. θρηνοῦντας ᾄδειν [hous dē ph. d. l. thrēnountas adein]), No bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or sad for any other reason; not even the nightingale, the swallow and the hoopoe, which they say sing mournfully for grief. Accordingly Proclus cannot bear that the swallow should be called ὀρθογόη [orthogoē] by Hesiod, and wants to read ὀρθοβόη [orthoboē], crying in the morning, so that the Poet may not seem to disagree with Plato. But Tzetzes answers otherwise: Ὑμεῖς δ' ἴσμεν καὶ δίχα μάρτυρος Πλάτωνος, ὅτι οὐδὲν ὄρνεον λυπούμενον ᾄδει· ἀλλὰ δεινῶς, καὶ ῥητορικῶς ὁ ποιητὴς τὴν λαλιὰν τῆς χελιδόνος θρῆνον εἶναι λέγει κατὰ τὸν μῦθον τῆς τοῦ Πανδίονος ἐκείνης θυγατρός [Hymeis d' ismen kai dicha martyros Platōnos, hoti ouden orneon lypoumenon adei; alla deinōs, kai rhētorikōs ho poiētēs tēn lalian tēs chelidonos thrēnon einai legei kata ton mython tēs tou Pandionos ekeinēs thygatros]. We know even without Plato as witness that no bird sings in grief. But the Poet skilfully and rhetorically calls the swallow's song a lament, in keeping with the fable of Pandion's daughter. So he, as though the swallow were said to mourn only because of the fable. Indeed, as Pausanias says in the Attica, σφίσι τὴν ἐς ἀηδόνα, καὶ χελιδόνα, μεταβολὴν ἐπεφήμισαν, ὅτι οἶμαι, καὶ αὗται αἱ ὄρνιθες ἐλεεινὸν, καὶ θρήνῳ ὅμοιον ᾄδουσιν [sphisi tēn es aēdona, kai chelidona, metabolēn epephēmisan, hoti oimai, kai hautai hai ornithes eleeinon, kai thrēnō homoion adousin], I think the common fable about Pandion's daughters, that one of them was changed into a nightingale and the other into a swallow, arose from the fact that each bird utters pitiful and mournful songs. [col. 65] Therefore nothing is to be changed in Hesiod. And the swallow would absurdly be called ὀρθοβόη [orthoboē] or ὀρθροβόη [orthroboē], since it is not a clamorous bird but one that twitters softly and ψιθυρίζουσα [psithyrizousa]. Hence Sidonius, book 2, letter 2, spoke of Procne twittering among the rafters. Likewise an unknown Poet in the Anthology,
Τραυλὰ μινυρομένη Πανδιονὶ κάμμορε φωνᾷ, [Traula minyromenē Pandioni kammore phōna,]

O wretched daughter of Pandion, twittering songs with lisping voice. Similar is what Pollux says in the chapter On the voices of birds, χελιδόνας ψιθυρίζειν [chelidonas psithyrizein], that swallows whisper. And that ψιθυρισμὸς [psithyrismos], or that twittering if you prefer, seems to have something in common with the complaints and murmurs that escape us in grief or for any other cause. Hence some of the ancients in Plutarch's Table Talk hold that by the swallow Pythagoras meant ψιθύρους [psithyrous], that is, whisperers or informers who secretly whisper into the ear. Still, what Plato says is true: swallows [II, 610] do not sing thus for grief. For a bird's song, however mournful it may seem, is the effect not of grief but of nature.

Now a few words on the migration of swallows in Ierem. VIII, 7. That they are migratory birds is known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers, and it has been observed in every age. Homer in the Εἰρεσιώνη [Eiresiōnē], quoted by Herodotus in his life,
Νεῦμαι σοι, νεῦμαι ἐνιαύσιος, ὥστε χελιδὼν, [Neumai soi, neumai eniausios, hōste chelidōn,]
I return to you every year, like the swallow. Anacreon, Ode 33,

Σὺ μὲν, φίλη χελιδὼν [Sy men, philē chelidōn] You, dear swallow, Ἐτησίη μολοῦσα [Etēsiē molousa], coming every year, Θέρει πλέκεις καλίην [Therei plekeis kaliēn], weave your nest in summer, Χειμῶσι δ' εἶς ἄφαντος [Cheimōsi d' eis aphantos]. And in winter you do not appear.
